notes.meaning: Habakkuk offers a prayer in the form of a song or psalm for his people to sing. The musical term Shigionoth refers to the style, tune, or instruments used to accompany the song. This prayer prepares God's people to keep trusting Him even in difficult times.

Habakkuk was filled with deep fear and reverence after hearing what God revealed about the coming judgment against Judah. He asks the Lord to renew His great saving deeds right in the middle of these troubled years. Knowing his people deserve punishment, he pleads that God will show mercy rather than anger alone.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Older Greek and Latin translations read 'in the midst of two animals,' which early Latin interpreters understood as a prophecy of Jesus Christ lying between an ox and a donkey in the manger.

notes.meaning: The prophet looks back to how God revealed His glory when He gave the law at Mount Sinai, near regions like Teman and Paran. Just as God appeared in shining majesty to make a covenant with His people then, He remains their holy Protector today. Remembering God's past greatness gives His people strong reasons to praise Him in dark days.

God's presence shines with a brilliant light brighter than the sun, flashing like rays from His hands. Even with all that brightness, the full greatness of His power stays hidden from human eyes because it is too wonderful to take in. God shows enough of His glory to comfort believers, yet keeps His ultimate majesty beyond human sight.

Pestilence and burning fever march before God like soldiers in His army carrying out His righteous will. When God delivered Israel in the past, He used deadly plagues to strike down their enemies and punish stubborn rebellion. His fearful power proves that no earthly enemy can stand in His way.

When the Lord steps forward, the whole earth shakes, and even the oldest mountains and hills crumble before Him. He looked over the nations and measured out the land to give it to His people Israel. Because God's ways never change, He still has the same power to deliver His people today.

The desert tribes of Cushan and Midian trembled with terror when they saw what God was doing for Israel. People living in tents along the desert borders knew they could not resist the Lord of heaven. God's mighty acts filled neighboring nations with dread and protected His chosen nation.

Habakkuk asks if God split the Red Sea and stopped the Jordan River because He was angry at the water. The real reason was God's love for His people, riding forward like a warrior king in chariots to bring them salvation. All of nature obeys the Lord when He moves to rescue those who belong to Him.

God drew out His bow and prepared His arrows to defeat the enemies of His chosen people. He did this to keep the sworn promises and covenant He had made with Israel's ancestors. He also split the dry earth with streams of fresh water to provide for His people in the wilderness.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars understand splitting the earth with rivers as poetic imagery describing a thunderstorm whose heavy downpours cause sudden flash floods across the dry ground.

notes.meaning: The great mountains shook at God's presence, just as Mount Sinai trembled when the Lord came down. The deep waters roared and lifted up their waves like hands raised in submission, parting to let Israel walk through safely. Every part of the natural world yields whenever God commands it.

The sun and moon stopped moving in the sky in the days of Joshua so God's people could defeat their enemies. The lightning and storm were like God's shining spear and flying arrows fighting on their side. God controls the lights of heaven to give victory to His servants.

The Lord marched across the land like a mighty conqueror leading His army into Canaan. He crushed the opposing nations like grain being beaten on a threshing floor. Israel won their victories not by their own strength, but because God went before them in power.

God marched out to deliver His chosen nation and bring victory through the leader He had chosen and set apart. He smashed the ruling powers of the wicked, tearing down their houses and stripping away their strength completely. All these past rescues pointed forward to God's ultimate work of salvation.

The enemy soldiers charged forward like a storm wind, eager to crush God's helpless people in secret. Instead, God turned their own weapons against them and struck down their leaders. Those who plot cruelty against God's people often fall into the very traps they prepared for others.

God led His people through the surging waters of the Red Sea as easily as a rider crosses on horseback. No barrier of deep water or human army could block the path He made for them. Looking back at this miracle reminded the prophet that God could clear any obstacle in the future too.

Thinking about the coming Babylonian invasion made Habakkuk shake with fear right to his bones. His body lost its strength, and his lips quivered at the thought of the terrible ruin his nation would suffer. Even so, he resolved to wait quietly on God, knowing that judgment would eventually fall upon the invaders.

The prophet describes total disaster, where all basic food supplies vanish from the land. The fruit trees die, grain crops fail in the fields, and the barns and sheepfolds sit completely empty. Habakkuk faces the harsh reality of war and famine with wide-open eyes.

Even when every earthly comfort and harvest is taken away, Habakkuk chooses to leap and sing for joy in the Lord Himself. His happiness does not depend on full barns, but on God who saves him. When we have lost every earthly blessing, God Himself remains our greatest treasure.

Habakkuk confesses that the Lord gives him all the strength he needs to keep going. God gives him sure-footed steps like a mountain deer, able to run safely across steep and dangerous ground. The note at the end shows this song was meant to be sung by the choir in public worship to encourage everyone's faith.
